subsystems.name: Reactor core
subsystems.role: produces heat by fissioning uranium fuel.
parts: uranium fuel elements (often high-assay low-enriched uranium)

subsystems.name: Power conversion
subsystems.role: turns reactor heat into electricity for the thrusters.
parts: closed Brayton turbo-alternator-compressor (helium–xenon) or Rankine loop

subsystems.name: Heat rejection
subsystems.role: dumps waste heat to space — the largest structure on the ship.

subsystems.name: Electric thrusters
subsystems.role: accelerate propellant ions to very high exhaust velocity.
parts: gridded ion or Hall-effect thruster units

subsystems.name: Propellant system
subsystems.role: stores and meters the propellant the thrusters expel.

subsystems.name: Shielding and structure
subsystems.role: keeps the reactor's neutrons and gamma rays away from payload and electronics.
parts: shadow shield (e.g. lithium hydride and tungsten)

buildSteps.title: Size the reactor and shield together
buildSteps.detail: The design sets how much power is needed and how much shielding is required to keep the payload within radiation limits.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the fuel and core
buildSteps.detail: Uranium fuel is clad and assembled with control drums and reflector into a compact core.

buildSteps.title: Build the power conversion loop
buildSteps.detail: A closed Brayton turbo-alternator on magnetic bearings is assembled and leak-tested with its helium–xenon working fluid.

buildSteps.title: Make the thrusters
buildSteps.detail: Ion optics grids or Hall thruster channels are machined and assembled, then tested on the ground with their power processing units.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: The reactor is mounted on a boom with its shadow shield, radiators are deployed on booms, and propellant tanks and thrusters are attached.

buildSteps.title: Ground-test the reactor
buildSteps.detail: The core is run at full power in a vacuum chamber, as NASA's Kilopower/KRUSTY test did in 2018, to prove it works before flight.

buildSteps.title: Launch shut down
buildSteps.detail: The reactor flies subcritical and only starts once safely in space.

buildSteps.title: Start up and commission
buildSteps.detail: The core is brought to power, the conversion loop is warmed, and each thruster is fired and checked.

buildSteps.title: Cruise on continuous thrust
buildSteps.detail: The ship thrusts for months at low acceleration, spiralling out of Earth orbit and building up the velocity a chemical rocket could not afford.

prerequisites.tech: Space fission reactors at hundreds of kilowatts
prerequisites.why: SNAP-10A flew in 1965 and Soviet TOPAZ reactors flew later, but at only a few kilowatts; Kilopower/KRUSTY proved a larger core on the ground.
ion and Hall thrusters have flown on Dawn, BepiColombo and Psyche at a few kilowatts; tens to hundreds of kilowatts have only been ground-tested.
rejecting megawatts of waste heat needs radiators far larger and lighter than anything flown.
years of continuous operation demand components that resist erosion and radiation damage.
months of unattended thrusting with minimal ground contact is beyond today's routine operations.

pathway.milestone: fission reactors and ion thrusters have flown, but never together
pathway.unlocks: the two core technologies are proven separately.

pathway.milestone: a flight demonstration of a 100 kW-class reactor and thruster system
pathway.unlocks: data on integrated operation, heat rejection and shielding.

pathway.milestone: an operational nuclear-electric cargo tug in Earth orbit
pathway.unlocks: moving heavy payloads to the Moon and Mars without giant chemical rockets.

pathway.milestone: megawatt-class ships for crewed Mars and outer-planet missions
